question:
Point $B$ is between $A$ and $C$ on $\overline{AC}$. $AB = 7$ and $BC = 12$.

Find $AC$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 120" width="360" height="120"><line x1="30" y1="60" x2="330" y2="60" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="30" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="30" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><circle cx="141" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="141" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><circle cx="330" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="330" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="85.5" y="89" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">7</text><text x="235.5" y="89" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">12</text></svg>
hint: The two smaller pieces join to make the whole segment.
solution:
By the **Segment Addition Postulate**, since $B$ is between $A$ and $C$:
$$AB + BC = AC$$
$$7 + 12 = AC$$
$$AC = 19$$

question:
Point $B$ is between $A$ and $C$ on $\overline{AC}$. $AC = 31$ and $AB = 12$.

Find $BC$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 120" width="360" height="120"><line x1="30" y1="60" x2="330" y2="60" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="30" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="30" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><circle cx="146.1" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="146.1" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><circle cx="330" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="330" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="88.1" y="89" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">12</text><text x="238.1" y="89" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">?</text><line x1="30" y1="32" x2="30" y2="26" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="330" y1="32" x2="330" y2="26" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="30" y1="26" x2="330" y2="26" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><text x="180" y="21" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">31</text></svg>
hint: Write the Segment Addition Postulate, then fill in what you know.
solution:
**What changed:** now the whole is given and one piece is unknown.

Segment Addition Postulate:
$$AB + BC = AC$$
$$12 + BC = 31$$
$$BC = 31 - 12 = 19$$

question:
Point $B$ is between $A$ and $C$ on $\overline{AC}$. $AB = x + 4$, $BC = 2x - 1$ and $AC = 24$.

Find $x$, $AB$ and $BC$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 120" width="360" height="120"><line x1="30" y1="60" x2="330" y2="60" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="30" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="30" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><circle cx="168" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="168" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><circle cx="330" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="330" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="99" y="89" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">x + 4</text><text x="249" y="89" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">2x − 1</text><line x1="30" y1="32" x2="30" y2="26" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="330" y1="32" x2="330" y2="26" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="30" y1="26" x2="330" y2="26" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><text x="180" y="21" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">24</text></svg>
hint: Write $AB + BC = AC$ with the expressions, then solve for $x$. Don't forget to substitute back.
solution:
**What changed:** the pieces are now algebraic expressions.

Segment Addition Postulate:
$$(x + 4) + (2x - 1) = 24$$
$$3x + 3 = 24$$
$$3x = 21 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 7$$

Substitute: $AB = 7 + 4 = 11$ and $BC = 2(7) - 1 = 13$.

Check: $11 + 13 = 24$ ✓

question:
Point $B$ is the **midpoint** of $\overline{AC}$. $AB = x + 4$ and $BC = 2x - 1$.

Find $x$, $AB$ and $AC$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 120" width="360" height="120"><line x1="30" y1="60" x2="330" y2="60" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="30" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="30" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><circle cx="180" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="180" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><circle cx="330" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="330" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="105" y="89" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">x + 4</text><text x="255" y="89" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">2x − 1</text></svg>
hint: A midpoint splits a segment into two congruent segments. Which two lengths are equal?
solution:
**What changed:** instead of being told $AC$, we are told $B$ is the midpoint. So the information gives an equation between the two **halves**.

Definition of midpoint: $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{BC}$, so $AB = BC$:
$$x + 4 = 2x - 1$$
$$5 = x$$

$AB = 5 + 4 = 9$ (and $BC = 2(5) - 1 = 9$ ✓).

The whole segment is twice a half:
$$AC = 2 \cdot AB = 18$$

question:
In the figure, points $P$, $Q$ and $R$ lie on a line in plane $M$, point $S$ lies in plane $M$ but not on the line, and point $T$ lies above plane $M$.

(a) Which three geometric terms are left **undefined** in geometry?

(b) Name the line in two different ways using the points shown.

(c) Name the ray with endpoint $Q$ that passes through $R$, and the ray opposite to it.

(d) Name a segment with endpoint $S$.

(e) Are $P$, $Q$ and $S$ collinear? Are $P$, $Q$ and $S$ coplanar? Are $P$, $Q$, $S$ and $T$ coplanar?
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 250" width="360" height="250"><polygon points="20,205 250,205 340,95 110,95" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="#3b82f6" fill-opacity="0.2"/><text x="132" y="114" fill="currentColor" font-size="15" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">M</text><line x1="50" y1="180" x2="305" y2="110" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="50,180 58.3,172.5 61,182.2" fill="currentColor"/><polygon points="305,110 296.7,117.5 294,107.8" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="95.9" cy="167.4" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="177.5" cy="145" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="259.1" cy="122.6" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="200" cy="185" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="150" cy="45" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="93.9" y="158.4" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">P</text><text x="175.5" y="136" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">Q</text><text x="257.1" y="113.6" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">R</text><text x="213" y="188" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">S</text><text x="163" y="48" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">T</text></svg>
hint: Collinear means on the same line; coplanar means in the same plane. For a ray, the **first** letter is the endpoint.
answer: (a) Point, line, plane. (b) e.g. $\overleftrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overleftrightarrow{QR}$ (also $\overleftrightarrow{PR}$, $\overleftrightarrow{RP}$, …). (c) $\overrightarrow{QR}$; opposite ray $\overrightarrow{QP}$. (d) e.g. $\overline{SQ}$. (e) $P$, $Q$, $S$ are not collinear but are coplanar; $P$, $Q$, $S$, $T$ are not coplanar.
solution:
**(a)** The undefined terms are **point**, **line** and **plane**. They are described, not defined, and every other term is defined from them.

**(b)** A line is named by any two points on it with a double arrow: $\overleftrightarrow{PQ}$, $\overleftrightarrow{QR}$, $\overleftrightarrow{PR}$, $\overleftrightarrow{QP}$, … all name the same line.

**(c)** The ray starting at $Q$ through $R$ is $\overrightarrow{QR}$ (endpoint first). Its opposite ray starts at the same endpoint and goes the other way: $\overrightarrow{QP}$. Together they form the line.

**(d)** For example $\overline{SQ}$ (or $\overline{SP}$, $\overline{SR}$, $\overline{ST}$).

**(e)**

* $P$, $Q$, $S$ are **not collinear**: $S$ is not on $\overleftrightarrow{PQ}$.
* $P$, $Q$, $S$ are **coplanar**: all three are in plane $M$.
* $P$, $Q$, $S$, $T$ are **not coplanar**: the only plane through $P$, $Q$ and $S$ is plane $M$ (three non-collinear points determine exactly one plane), and $T$ is not in it.

question:
Point $D$ is in the interior of $\angle ABC$. $m\angle ABD = (2x + 10)^\circ$, $m\angle DBC = (3x - 5)^\circ$ and $m\angle ABC = 105^\circ$.

(a) Find $x$.

(b) Find $m\angle ABD$ and $m\angle DBC$.

(c) Classify each of $\angle ABD$, $\angle DBC$ and $\angle ABC$ as acute, right, obtuse or straight.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 230" width="360" height="230"><line x1="80" y1="205" x2="340" y2="205" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="340,205 330,210 330,200" fill="currentColor"/><line x1="80" y1="205" x2="208.6" y2="51.8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="208.6,51.8 206,62.7 198.3,56.2" fill="currentColor"/><line x1="80" y1="205" x2="36" y2="40.8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="36,40.8 43.4,49.2 33.8,51.7" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="80" cy="205" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="68" y="218" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="330" y="228" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="212.6" y="42.8" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">D</text><text x="20" y="51.8" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><path d="M130 205 A50 50 0 0 0 112.1 166.7" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="166.1" y="169.9" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">(2x + 10)°</text><path d="M105.7 174.4 A40 40 0 0 0 69.6 166.4" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="97.7" y="129.9" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">(3x − 5)°</text></svg>
hint: Use the Angle Addition Postulate: $m\angle ABD + m\angle DBC = m\angle ABC$.
answer: (a) $x = 20$ (b) $m\angle ABD = 50^\circ$, $m\angle DBC = 55^\circ$ (c) $\angle ABD$ acute, $\angle DBC$ acute, $\angle ABC$ obtuse
solution:
**(a)** By the **Angle Addition Postulate**:
$$(2x + 10) + (3x - 5) = 105$$
$$5x + 5 = 105 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 5x = 100 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 20$$

**(b)** $m\angle ABD = 2(20) + 10 = 50^\circ$ and $m\angle DBC = 3(20) - 5 = 55^\circ$.

Check: $50^\circ + 55^\circ = 105^\circ$ ✓

**(c)**

* $\angle ABD$: $0^\circ < 50^\circ < 90^\circ$, **acute**.
* $\angle DBC$: $55^\circ$, **acute**.
* $\angle ABC$: $90^\circ < 105^\circ < 180^\circ$, **obtuse**.

(Two acute angles can add up to an obtuse angle.)

question:
Lines $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overleftrightarrow{CD}$ intersect at $E$. $m\angle AEC = 38^\circ$.

(a) Find $m\angle 1$, $m\angle 2$ and $m\angle 3$. Give a reason for each.

(b) Name two pairs of vertical angles and two linear pairs.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 240" width="360" height="240"><line x1="30" y1="120" x2="330" y2="120" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="69.7" y1="33.8" x2="290.3" y2="206.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="30" cy="120" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="330" cy="120" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="69.7" cy="33.8" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="290.3" cy="206.2" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="180" cy="120" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><text x="28" y="113" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="332" y="113" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="65.7" y="26.8" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="294.3" y="229.2" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">D</text><text x="190" y="113" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">E</text><path d="M140 120 A40 40 0 0 1 148.5 95.4" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="121.4" y="104.8" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">38°</text><text x="192.4" y="89.1" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">1</text><text x="215.9" y="137.4" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">2</text><text x="167.6" y="160.9" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">3</text></svg>
hint: Angles next to each other along a straight line form a linear pair (they add to $180^\circ$). Angles opposite each other at $E$ are vertical angles (congruent).
answer: (a) $m\angle 1 = 142^\circ$, $m\angle 2 = 38^\circ$, $m\angle 3 = 142^\circ$ (b) Vertical: $\angle AEC$ and $\angle 2$ ($\angle BED$); $\angle 1$ ($\angle CEB$) and $\angle 3$ ($\angle DEA$). Linear pairs: e.g. $\angle AEC$ and $\angle 1$; $\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ (also $\angle 2$ and $\angle 3$; $\angle 3$ and $\angle AEC$).
solution:
**(a)**

* $\angle AEC$ and $\angle 1$ ($\angle CEB$) form a **linear pair** ($\overrightarrow{EA}$ and $\overrightarrow{EB}$ are opposite rays), so they are supplementary: $m\angle 1 = 180^\circ - 38^\circ = 142^\circ$.
* $\angle 2$ ($\angle BED$) and $\angle AEC$ are **vertical angles**, so they are congruent: $m\angle 2 = 38^\circ$.
* $\angle 3$ ($\angle DEA$) and $\angle 1$ are vertical angles: $m\angle 3 = 142^\circ$.

Check: $38 + 142 + 38 + 142 = 360$ ✓ (angles around a point).

**(b)** Vertical angles (non-adjacent, opposite each other across $E$): $\angle AEC$ and $\angle BED$; $\angle CEB$ and $\angle DEA$.

Linear pairs (adjacent, with non-common sides forming a line): $\angle AEC$ and $\angle CEB$; $\angle CEB$ and $\angle BED$; $\angle BED$ and $\angle DEA$; $\angle DEA$ and $\angle AEC$.

question:
$M$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$. $AM = 2x + 5$ and $AB = 7x - 5$. Find $AB$.

Diego's working is shown below.

$M$ is the midpoint, so $AM = AB$.

$2x + 5 = 7x - 5$

$10 = 5x$, so $x = 2$

$AB = 7(2) - 5 = 9$

(a) Explain the mistake Diego made.

(b) How could Diego have spotted that his answer was wrong?

(c) Find the correct value of $x$ and the length $AB$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 120" width="360" height="120"><line x1="30" y1="60" x2="330" y2="60" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="30" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="30" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><circle cx="180" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="180" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">M</text><circle cx="330" cy="60" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="330" y="49" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="105" y="89" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">2x + 5</text><line x1="30" y1="32" x2="30" y2="26" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="330" y1="32" x2="330" y2="26" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="30" y1="26" x2="330" y2="26" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><text x="180" y="21" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">7x − 5</text></svg>
hint: A midpoint splits a segment into two equal halves. How does the whole compare with one half?
answer: (a) He set the half $AM$ equal to the whole $AB$; it should be $AB = 2 \cdot AM$ (or $AM = MB$). (b) His values give $AM = 9$ and $AB = 9$, so $MB = 0$, which is impossible. (c) $x = 5$, $AB = 30$
solution:
**(a)** The error is the first line. A midpoint makes the two **halves** congruent, $AM = MB$; it does not make a half equal to the whole. Since $AM + MB = AB$ (Segment Addition) and $AM = MB$:
$$AB = 2 \cdot AM$$

**(b)** With $x = 2$: $AM = 2(2) + 5 = 9$ and $AB = 9$. Then $MB = AB - AM = 0$, so $M$ would be the same point as $B$, which is not a midpoint. Always substitute back and check the answer makes sense.

**(c)**
$$2(2x + 5) = 7x - 5$$
$$4x + 10 = 7x - 5$$
$$15 = 3x \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 5$$

$AM = 2(5) + 5 = 15$ and $AB = 7(5) - 5 = 30$ ✓ (twice $AM$).

question:
Given: $M$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ and $AB = 12$. Find $AM$.

Owen's work is shown below. Each line has a statement and a reason.

1. $AM \cong MB$ (Definition of midpoint)
2. $AM + MB = AB$ (Segment Addition Postulate)
3. $AM + AM = 12$ (Substitution)
4. $AM = 6$ (Division Property of Equality)

(a) One line uses incorrect notation. Which line is it, and what is wrong with it?

(b) Write two correct versions of that statement: one about segments and one about lengths.
hint: Is $AM$ (no bar) a figure or a number? Which symbol goes with figures, and which goes with numbers?
answer: (a) Line 1: $AM$ and $MB$ are lengths (numbers), so they are equal, not congruent. (b) $\overline{AM} \cong \overline{MB}$ (segments) or $AM = MB$ (lengths).
solution:
**(a)** Line 1 is wrong. Without a bar, $AM$ means the **length** of the segment, which is a number. Numbers are **equal** ($=$); only figures (segments, angles, triangles) are **congruent** ($\cong$). Writing $AM \cong MB$ mixes a symbol for figures with numbers.

**(b)**

* About segments (figures): $\overline{AM} \cong \overline{MB}$
* About lengths (numbers): $AM = MB$

Either is a correct use of the definition of midpoint. (The rest of Owen's work is fine: lines 2 to 4 correctly use lengths and $=$, giving $AM = 6$.)

The same rule applies to angles: $\angle 1 \cong \angle 2$ but $m\angle 1 = m\angle 2$.

question:
Points $P$, $Q$ and $R$ lie on a line in that order, as shown.

Ava says: "$\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{QP}$ are the same ray, because both rays contain the points $P$ and $Q$."

(a) Is Ava correct? Explain, describing each ray.

(b) Decide whether each statement is true or false, and explain:

(i) $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{PR}$ are the same ray.

(ii) $\overline{PQ}$ and $\overline{QP}$ are the same segment.

(iii) $\overrightarrow{QP}$ and $\overrightarrow{QR}$ are opposite rays.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 90" width="360" height="90"><line x1="20" y1="45" x2="340" y2="45" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="20,45 30,40 30,50" fill="currentColor"/><polygon points="340,45 330,50 330,40" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="90" cy="45" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="90" y="34" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">P</text><circle cx="180" cy="45" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="180" y="34" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">Q</text><circle cx="270" cy="45" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="270" y="34" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">R</text></svg>
hint: For a ray, the first letter is the endpoint and the ray goes on forever through the second point. Where does each ray start, and which way does it go?
answer: (a) No. $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ starts at $P$ and goes through $Q$ toward $R$ forever; $\overrightarrow{QP}$ starts at $Q$ and goes through $P$ in the other direction. They have different endpoints and directions (they share only $\overline{PQ}$). (b)(i) True (ii) True (iii) True
solution:
**(a)** Ava is **not correct**. A ray has one endpoint, named first, and extends forever in one direction.

* $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ starts at $P$ and goes through $Q$, then on through $R$ and beyond to the right.
* $\overrightarrow{QP}$ starts at $Q$ and goes through $P$ and beyond to the left.

They have different endpoints and point in opposite directions. They only overlap in the segment $\overline{PQ}$; for example, $R$ is on $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ but not on $\overrightarrow{QP}$.

**(b)**

(i) **True.** Both start at $P$ and go in the same direction ($R$ is beyond $Q$), so they are the same set of points.

(ii) **True.** A segment has two endpoints and no direction, so $\overline{PQ}$ and $\overline{QP}$ name the same figure (the same is true for lines: $\overleftrightarrow{PQ} = \overleftrightarrow{QP}$).

(iii) **True.** They share the endpoint $Q$, go in opposite directions, and together form the line, which is the definition of opposite rays.

hint: Adjacent angles share a vertex and a side **and** have no interior points in common. A linear pair must be adjacent **and** its non-common sides must be opposite rays.
answer: Mia is wrong: the interiors overlap ($\angle ABD$ lies inside $\angle ABC$), so they are not adjacent. Leo is wrong: the angles are supplementary but are not adjacent (no common vertex or side), so they are not a linear pair.
solution:
**Mia.** Definition: adjacent angles are two coplanar angles with a common vertex and a common side, but **no common interior points**.

$\angle ABD$ and $\angle ABC$ do share vertex $B$ and side $\overrightarrow{BA}$, but every interior point of $\angle ABD$ is also inside $\angle ABC$ (because $D$ is in the interior of $\angle ABC$). So they are **not** adjacent. Mia is **incorrect**. (The adjacent pair in Figure 1 is $\angle ABD$ and $\angle DBC$.)

**Leo.** Definition: a linear pair is a pair of **adjacent** angles whose non-common sides are **opposite rays**. Such angles are always supplementary, but supplementary angles need not be a linear pair.

$\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ are supplementary ($65^\circ + 115^\circ = 180^\circ$), but they have different vertices and no common side, so they are not adjacent and cannot be a linear pair. Leo is **incorrect**; the correct description is "$\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ are supplementary angles".

question:
A straight stretch of highway runs between town $A$ at mile marker 14 and town $C$ at mile marker 86.

(a) A gas station $B$ lies between the towns and is 3 times as far from $A$ as it is from $C$. At which mile marker is the gas station?

(b) A rest stop $M$ is at the midpoint of $\overline{AC}$. At which mile marker is the rest stop?

(c) How far is it from the rest stop to the gas station?
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 110" width="360" height="110"><line x1="20" y1="55" x2="340" y2="55" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="30" cy="55" r="4" fill="currentColor"/><text x="30" y="44" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="30" y="86" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">mile 14</text><circle cx="330" cy="55" r="4" fill="currentColor"/><text x="330" y="44" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="330" y="86" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">mile 86</text></svg>
hint: Let $BC = d$ miles. Then $AB = 3d$, and Segment Addition gives $AB + BC = AC$.
solution:
$AC = 86 - 14 = 72$ miles.

**(a)** Let $BC = d$. Then $AB = 3d$, and by Segment Addition:
$$3d + d = 72 \quad\Rightarrow\quad d = 18$$

So $AB = 54$ miles, and the gas station is at mile $14 + 54 = 68$. (Check: $86 - 68 = 18$ ✓)

**(b)** The midpoint is halfway: $AM = \frac{1}{2}(72) = 36$, so $M$ is at mile $14 + 36 = 50$. (Or average the markers: $\frac{14 + 86}{2} = 50$.)

**(c)** $M$ (mile 50) is between $A$ and $B$ (mile 68), so by Segment Addition $MB = AB - AM = 54 - 36 = 18$ miles.

parts.prompt: Do $\angle ABD$ and $\angle DBE$ form a linear pair? Explain, and verify using their measures.

hint: An angle bisector creates two congruent angles. Angles whose non-common sides are opposite rays form a linear pair.
answer: (a) $x = 11$ (b) $m\angle ABC = 94^\circ$, obtuse (c) $m\angle CBE = 86^\circ$ (d) Yes: they are adjacent (common side $\overrightarrow{BD}$) and their non-common sides $\overrightarrow{BA}$, $\overrightarrow{BE}$ are opposite rays; $47^\circ + 133^\circ = 180^\circ$.
solution:
**(a)** $\overrightarrow{BD}$ bisects $\angle ABC$, so $\angle ABD \cong \angle DBC$ and $m\angle ABD = m\angle DBC$ (1 pt for the equation):
$$5x - 8 = 3x + 14$$
$$2x = 22 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 11 \quad \text{(1 pt)}$$

**(b)** $m\angle ABD = 5(11) - 8 = 47^\circ$, so by Angle Addition $m\angle ABC = 47^\circ + 47^\circ = 94^\circ$. It is **obtuse** ($90^\circ < 94^\circ < 180^\circ$). (1 pt)

**(c)** $\overrightarrow{BA}$ and $\overrightarrow{BE}$ are opposite rays, so $\angle ABC$ and $\angle CBE$ form a linear pair and are supplementary:
$$m\angle CBE = 180^\circ - 94^\circ = 86^\circ \quad \text{(1 pt)}$$

**(d)** **Yes.** $\angle ABD$ and $\angle DBE$ share vertex $B$ and side $\overrightarrow{BD}$ with no common interior points, so they are adjacent; their non-common sides $\overrightarrow{BA}$ and $\overrightarrow{BE}$ are opposite rays. So they form a linear pair. (1 pt)

Verify: by Angle Addition, $m\angle DBE = m\angle DBC + m\angle CBE = 47^\circ + 86^\circ = 133^\circ$, and $47^\circ + 133^\circ = 180^\circ$ ✓ (1 pt)

question:
On the coordinate plane, $A(-3, 5)$ and $B(7, -1)$.

(a) Find the coordinates of $M$, the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$.

(b) $B$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AC}$. Find the coordinates of $C$.

(c) Use the distance formula to find $AB$, $BC$ and $AC$ in simplest radical form, and show that they satisfy the Segment Addition Postulate.
hint: Midpoint: average the $x$-coordinates and average the $y$-coordinates. For (b), the step from $A$ to $B$ is repeated to get from $B$ to $C$.
solution:
**(a)**
$$M = \left(\frac{-3 + 7}{2}, \frac{5 + (-1)}{2}\right) = (2, 2)$$

**(b)** From $A$ to $B$ the change is $+10$ in $x$ and $-6$ in $y$. $B$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AC}$, so the same change takes $B$ to $C$:
$$C = (7 + 10, -1 - 6) = (17, -7)$$

Check: midpoint of $A(-3, 5)$ and $C(17, -7)$ is $\left(\frac{14}{2}, \frac{-2}{2}\right) = (7, -1) = B$ ✓

**(c)**
$$AB = \sqrt{(7 - (-3))^2 + (-1 - 5)^2} = \sqrt{100 + 36} = \sqrt{136} = 2\sqrt{34}$$
$$BC = \sqrt{(17 - 7)^2 + (-7 - (-1))^2} = \sqrt{100 + 36} = 2\sqrt{34}$$
$$AC = \sqrt{(17 - (-3))^2 + (-7 - 5)^2} = \sqrt{400 + 144} = \sqrt{544} = 4\sqrt{34}$$

Segment Addition: $AB + BC = 2\sqrt{34} + 2\sqrt{34} = 4\sqrt{34} = AC$ ✓, consistent with $B$ lying between $A$ and $C$ (and $AB = BC$, as $B$ is the midpoint).

question:
$\angle PQR$ and $\angle RQS$ form a linear pair. $m\angle PQR = (x^2 + 4x)^\circ$ and $m\angle RQS = (6x + 36)^\circ$.

(a) Write and solve an equation to find the possible values of $x$.

(b) Which value of $x$ gives a valid figure? Explain why the other value must be rejected.

(c) Find the measure of each angle.
hint: Linear pair $\Rightarrow$ supplementary. You will get a quadratic equation; rearrange it to $= 0$ and factor.
answer: (a) $x^2 + 10x - 144 = 0$, so $x = 8$ or $x = -18$ (b) $x = 8$; $x = -18$ gives $m\angle RQS = -72^\circ$, which is impossible. (c) $m\angle PQR = 96^\circ$, $m\angle RQS = 84^\circ$
solution:
**(a)** Angles in a linear pair are supplementary:
$$(x^2 + 4x) + (6x + 36) = 180$$
$$x^2 + 10x + 36 - 180 = 0$$
$$x^2 + 10x - 144 = 0$$

Find two numbers with product $-144$ and sum $10$: $18$ and $-8$.
$$(x + 18)(x - 8) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = -18 \text{ or } x = 8$$

**(b)** Check each value in **both** angle expressions:

* $x = 8$: $m\angle PQR = 64 + 32 = 96^\circ$ and $m\angle RQS = 48 + 36 = 84^\circ$. Both positive ✓
* $x = -18$: $m\angle PQR = 324 - 72 = 252^\circ$ and $m\angle RQS = -108 + 36 = -72^\circ$. An angle measure cannot be negative (and each angle of a linear pair must be less than $180^\circ$), so reject $x = -18$.

**(c)** $m\angle PQR = 96^\circ$ (obtuse) and $m\angle RQS = 84^\circ$ (acute). Check: $96 + 84 = 180$ ✓

question:
(a) The supplement of an angle measures $12^\circ$ more than three times the complement of the angle. Find the measure of the angle.

(b) Explain why only acute angles have complements, but every angle with measure between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ has a supplement.

(c) Show that, for any acute angle, its supplement is always exactly $90^\circ$ more than its complement.
hint: Let the angle be $x^\circ$. Its complement is $(90 - x)^\circ$ and its supplement is $(180 - x)^\circ$.
answer: (a) $51^\circ$ (b) A complement $90 - x$ must be positive, so $x < 90$; a supplement $180 - x$ is positive whenever $x < 180$. (c) $(180 - x) - (90 - x) = 90$.
solution:
Let the angle measure $x^\circ$. By definition, complementary angles add to $90^\circ$ and supplementary angles add to $180^\circ$.

**(a)** Complement: $90 - x$. Supplement: $180 - x$.
$$180 - x = 3(90 - x) + 12$$
$$180 - x = 270 - 3x + 12$$
$$180 - x = 282 - 3x$$
$$2x = 102 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 51$$

Check: complement $39^\circ$, supplement $129^\circ$, and $3(39) + 12 = 129$ ✓. The angle measures $51^\circ$.

**(b)** An angle measure must be positive. The complement $90 - x$ is positive only when $x < 90$, i.e. the angle is acute. The supplement $180 - x$ is positive for every $x < 180$, so every angle between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ (acute, right or obtuse) has a supplement.

**(c)** For an acute angle $x^\circ$:
$$(180 - x) - (90 - x) = 180 - x - 90 + x = 90$$
So the supplement is always $90^\circ$ more than the complement, whatever the acute angle. (Check with (a): $129 - 39 = 90$ ✓)

question:
Points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on a line in that order. $AC = 20$, $BD = 26$ and $AD = 36$.

$M$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ and $N$ is the midpoint of $\overline{CD}$.

(a) Find $MN$.

(b) Prove that, for **any** four points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ on a line in that order, with $M$ and $N$ the midpoints of $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$,
$$MN = \frac{AD + BC}{2}$$
hint: Use Segment Addition to find $AB$, $BC$ and $CD$ first. For the proof, place the points on a number line with coordinates $a < b < c < d$.
answer: (a) $MN = 23$ (b) With coordinates $a < b < c < d$: $MN = \frac{c + d}{2} - \frac{a + b}{2} = \frac{(d - a) + (c - b)}{2} = \frac{AD + BC}{2}$.
solution:
**(a)** Segment Addition along the line:

* $AC + CD = AD$, so $CD = 36 - 20 = 16$.
* $AB + BD = AD$, so $AB = 36 - 26 = 10$.
* $AB + BC + CD = AD$, so $BC = 36 - 10 - 16 = 10$.

$M$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$: $MB = 5$. $N$ is the midpoint of $\overline{CD}$: $CN = 8$.

$M$, $B$, $C$, $N$ are in that order, so
$$MN = MB + BC + CN = 5 + 10 + 8 = 23$$

**(b)** Place the line on a number line, with coordinates $a < b < c < d$ for $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ (Ruler Postulate). The distance between two points is the absolute value of the difference of their coordinates.

Midpoints: $M$ has coordinate $\frac{a + b}{2}$, $N$ has coordinate $\frac{c + d}{2}$. Since $a + b < c + d$, $N$ is to the right of $M$:
$$MN = \frac{c + d}{2} - \frac{a + b}{2} = \frac{(d - a) + (c - b)}{2}$$

But $d - a = AD$ and $c - b = BC$, so
$$MN = \frac{AD + BC}{2} \qquad \blacksquare$$

Check with (a): $\frac{36 + 10}{2} = 23$ ✓

question:
$\angle ABD$ and $\angle DBC$ form a linear pair. $\overrightarrow{BE}$ bisects $\angle ABD$ and $\overrightarrow{BF}$ bisects $\angle DBC$.

(a) Prove that $\overrightarrow{BE} \perp \overrightarrow{BF}$, i.e. that $m\angle EBF = 90^\circ$. Give a reason for each step.

(b) Does the result still hold if $\angle ABD$ and $\angle DBC$ are adjacent but **not** a linear pair? Explain.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 200" width="360" height="200"><line x1="20" y1="170" x2="340" y2="170" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="20,170 30,165 30,175" fill="currentColor"/><polygon points="340,170 330,175 330,165" fill="currentColor"/><line x1="180" y1="170" x2="245.7" y2="46.4" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="245.7,46.4 245.4,57.6 236.6,52.9" fill="currentColor"/><line x1="180" y1="170" x2="113" y2="58.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><polygon points="113,58.6 121.5,64 113.8,68.6" fill="currentColor"/><line x1="180" y1="170" x2="291.4" y2="103" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><polygon points="291.4,103 286,111.5 281.4,103.8" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="180" cy="170" r="3.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="180" y="195" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="26" y="195" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="334" y="195" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="249.7" y="39.4" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">D</text><text x="101" y="57.6" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">E</text><text x="303.4" y="106" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">F</text></svg>
hint: Let $m\angle ABD = 2a$ and $m\angle DBC = 2c$. What do you know about $2a + 2c$? Then use the Angle Addition Postulate for $\angle EBF$.
answer: (a) Let $m\angle ABD = 2a$, $m\angle DBC = 2c$; linear pair gives $2a + 2c = 180$; bisectors give $m\angle EBD = a$, $m\angle DBF = c$; Angle Addition gives $m\angle EBF = a + c = 90^\circ$. (b) No: in general $m\angle EBF = \frac{1}{2}m\angle ABC$, which is $90^\circ$ only when $m\angle ABC = 180^\circ$, i.e. a linear pair.
solution:
**(a)** Let $m\angle ABD = 2a$ and $m\angle DBC = 2c$.

1. $\angle ABD$ and $\angle DBC$ form a linear pair, so they are supplementary (Linear Pair Postulate):
$$2a + 2c = 180 \quad\Rightarrow\quad a + c = 90$$

2. $\overrightarrow{BE}$ bisects $\angle ABD$, so $m\angle EBD = \frac{1}{2}(2a) = a$ (definition of angle bisector).

3. $\overrightarrow{BF}$ bisects $\angle DBC$, so $m\angle DBF = \frac{1}{2}(2c) = c$ (definition of angle bisector).

4. $D$ is in the interior of $\angle EBF$, so by the **Angle Addition Postulate**:
$$m\angle EBF = m\angle EBD + m\angle DBF = a + c = 90^\circ$$

5. So $\angle EBF$ is a right angle and $\overrightarrow{BE} \perp \overrightarrow{BF}$ (definition of perpendicular). $\blacksquare$

**(b)** **No.** If $\angle ABD$ and $\angle DBC$ are adjacent with $m\angle ABC = 2a + 2c$, the same steps give
$$m\angle EBF = a + c = \tfrac{1}{2}\,m\angle ABC$$
This equals $90^\circ$ only when $m\angle ABC = 180^\circ$, which is exactly when $\overrightarrow{BA}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ are opposite rays, i.e. the angles form a linear pair. For example, if $m\angle ABD = 40^\circ$ and $m\angle DBC = 60^\circ$, then $m\angle EBF = 20^\circ + 30^\circ = 50^\circ$.
